metadata.title: Student test-taking effort in low-stakes assessments: evidence from the English version of the PISA 2015 science test

survey_design.weight_variable_name: house weights (sum equals sample size); 80 PISA replicates
survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study used PISA 2015 microdata for the science domain, restricted to six English-administering countries and to assessment forms without collaborative problem solving clusters. For the expectancy-value regressions and the variance/correlation analyses, the authors applied house weighting for both the computation of statistics and the replications, and they based standard errors on PISA’s 80 replicate weights. The analyses were further conditioned on response-time based effort indices derived from computer-based science items, with additional robustness subsamples excluding students with not-reached items and/or with total session response time above 3000s. Because the models are not standard ML learners but mixture-model-based effort classification and beta regressions, the paper still explicitly follows OECD/PISA plausible value and replication guidance for weighted inference.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: Used PISA 2015 computer-based science items administered in English in six selected English-speaking countries (Australia, Canada, United Kingdom, Ireland, New Zealand, United States). Selected assessment forms that contained only science, mathematics and/or reading clusters (excluding collaborative problem solving clusters in countries where it was present). For effort estimation, analyzed response times at four cluster positions; trimmed item RT distributions at the 99% level (excluded the right tail) and excluded items whose RT distributions could not be described by the expected two-class finite mixture model or whose latent classes did not match the assumed effortful vs non-effortful interpretation. For robustness checks, recomputed results on subsamples excluding students with any not-reached items and on subsamples with total session response time < 3000s (50 minutes).

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2015 Science (computer-based), English version; cluster positions 1-4
main_findings.target_variable: Test-taking effort (average posterior probability of being effortful)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Beta regression (house-weighted; SEs via 80 PISA replicates). Pseudo R² for expectancy-value predictors: ~0.03 (cluster 1), 0.04 (cluster 2), 0.06 (cluster 3), 0.07 (cluster 4) on average; key coefficient directions: ENVAWARE positive; INTBRSCI and JOYSCIE positive; ANXTEST mostly negligible; SCIEACT negative. Additional analysis (Science achievement (Plausible Values)): Correlations between effort and science achievement (weighted): cluster 1 average ~0.39 (range 0.37–0.42) increasing to cluster 4 average ~0.56 (range 0.50–0.59). Variance explained by effort (gross %): ~11.79% at cluster 1 increasing to ~26.68% at cluster 4; net % (after covariates) up to ~14.40% at cluster 4 (e.g., Canada net 11.76%); joint % with all predictors up to ~18.41% at cluster 4 (e.g., New Zealand).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2015 Science (computer-based), English version the study leveraged environmental awareness (ENVAWARE), interest in broad science (INTBRSCI), enjoyment of science (JOYSCIE), test anxiety (ANXTEST), and science activities (SCIEACT) to predict test-taking effort (average posterior probability of being effortful), finding that expectancy-value proxies had only a trivial explanatory power (average pseudo R² up to ~0.07) while environmental awareness and intrinsic value proxies were generally positively associated with effort and science activities were negatively associated. This indicates that improving students’ science-related interest/enjoyment and perceived relevance may help engagement, but most effort variation likely comes from factors beyond the measured expectancy-value attitudes.

data.outcome_summary: This study analyzes test-taking engagement in the PISA 2015 science assessment (computer-based, English version) using response times from science items administered in four cluster positions. The authors selected six English-speaking countries (AUS, CAN, GBR, IRL, NZL, USA) and derived an effort index by fitting a two-class finite mixture model to item RT distributions (99% trimmed RTs), then aggregating posterior probabilities of belonging to the effortful class into a global effort measure. Effort decreased toward the end of the test (mean effort probability dropping from about 0.94 to 0.88 in session 1, and from 0.90 to 0.85 in session 2). Expectancy-value proxies explained only a trivial amount of effort variability (average pseudo R² up to ~0.07). Critically, effort correlated strongly with science achievement and the association increased across clusters (from ~0.39 to ~0.56), with gross variance explained rising from ~11.79% to ~26.68% by the last cluster. The study uses house weighting and PISA replicate-based standard errors; however, the effort–achievement link is correlational and the effort measure may conflate disengagement with fatigue or perseverance.
data.null_fields_interpretation: The paper does not train standard machine-learning predictive algorithms (e.g., Random Forest/XGBoost/SVM) on the ILSA data; instead it uses a two-class finite mixture model to classify effort from response-time distributions and then applies beta regression and correlation/variance decomposition to relate effort to achievement. Therefore, the ML technique fields are left empty rather than incorrectly listing non-ML statistical models.
